section_summary: This section follows American and British efforts to respond jointly to Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, especially its sales quotas and oil stockholding requirements. Repeated copies of telegrams, interview notes, and memoranda record signs that Japanese officials might consider adjustments, while foreign companies sought assurances before committing to 1935 business plans. The final telegram reports informal Anglo-American representations to the Japanese Foreign Office and a possible meeting between Japanese officials and senior oil company representatives.

people.name: Ray Atherton
people.role: Counselor of Embassy in London; later chargé d’affaires ad interim

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: Kurusu
people.role: Chief of the Bureau of Commercial Affairs, Japanese Foreign Office

people.name: Yoshino
people.role: Japanese Vice Minister of Commerce and Industry

people.name: Fukuda
people.role: Chief of the Mining Bureau, Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry

people.name: Horie
people.role: Participant in the November 20 Mining Bureau conference

people.name: Sakai
people.role: Participant in the November 20 Mining Bureau conference

people.name: Morita
people.role: Standard-Vacuum Oil Company participant in the November 20 Mining Bureau conference

people.name: Hashimoto
people.role: Japan Oil Company figure and member of the House of Peers

people.name: Millard
people.role: Participant in U.S. Embassy discussions with the British Foreign Office

people.name: Dooman
people.role: U.S. official discussing oil policy with the British Foreign Office

people.name: Lickover
people.role: U.S. representative at the December 27 meeting with Kurusu

subfiles.title: Instructions to the Embassy in London on coordinated oil representations
subfiles.about: The Department urges a common Anglo-American approach and asks London to clarify the proposed instructions to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Hull calls for parallel action and says London should serve as the clearing point.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram No. 274 on proposed informal representations
subfiles.about: Grew recommends coordinated informal responses to Japan’s unsatisfactory explanation of its petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu suggests that foreign and Japanese oil companies protest together. Grew proposes oral representations, coordinated with Britain, concerning uncertain quotas, limits on foreign refining, and costly stockholding requirements. He argues that continued diplomatic support could help the companies reach a compromise without forcing Japanese officials into a public retreat.

subfiles.title: Department’s interim reply to Grew telegram No. 274
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Grew’s proposal and promises a further response.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it is considering the proposal and will reply soon.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Grew telegram No. 274
subfiles.about: This copy repeats Grew’s proposed informal representations about quotas, refining, and stockholding.
subfiles.summary: Grew urges a coordinated British and American oral approach that preserves diplomatic support for the oil companies. His suggested points challenge the uncertainty of annual quotas, restrictions on foreign participation in refining, and the cost of required oil stocks.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1086 on Japanese and Manchurian oil monopolies
subfiles.about: Atherton reports conveying the Department’s oil monopoly instructions orally to the British Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Atherton confirms that the Foreign Office received the substance of the instructions.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of despatch No. 1086
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of Atherton’s report on oral communication with the British Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Repeats Atherton’s confirmation that the instructions were conveyed orally.

subfiles.title: Triplicate of despatch No. 1086
subfiles.about: Triplicate copy of Atherton’s report on oral communication with the British Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Repeats Atherton’s confirmation that the instructions were conveyed orally.

subfiles.title: Quadruplicate of despatch No. 1086
subfiles.about: Quadruplicate copy of Atherton’s report on oral communication with the British Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Repeats Atherton’s confirmation that the instructions were conveyed orally.

subfiles.title: Coe letter forwarding notes of a Japanese oil law interview
subfiles.about: Coe forwards interview notes and expresses cautious hope that Japan may moderate application of its petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Coe sends duplicate notes and thanks the Department for continued efforts.

subfiles.title: Notes of Yoshino–Kurusu interview with Goold and Ely
subfiles.about: Japanese officials discuss guarantees, refining, quotas, stockholding, and conditional 1935 plans with foreign oil representatives.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino says Japan wants foreign oil companies to remain and suggests a long term guarantee of existing trade. He promises no discrimination against foreign refining but declines to revise current quotas. Kurusu says documented commercial evidence of the stockholding burden could prompt reconsideration, while Yoshino offers to accept conditional business plans for 1935.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of meeting at Shokosho
subfiles.about: Fukuda refuses to postpone Standard-Vacuum’s complete 1935 plan and warns of penalties.
subfiles.summary: Fukuda insists on immediate filing, separates enforcement from diplomatic talks, and rejects a higher current quota. Company representatives say they lack authority to commit to the resulting expense.

subfiles.title: Second copy of Yoshino–Kurusu interview notes
subfiles.about: A second copy records the November 20 discussion of Japan’s petroleum controls with Goold and Ely.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino offers assurances on continued foreign trade and possible refining while maintaining existing quotas. Kurusu suggests that detailed cost evidence might persuade the government to reconsider stockholding requirements. The officials also discuss a sales pool and conditional filing of 1935 plans.

subfiles.title: Second copy of Shokosho meeting memorandum
subfiles.about: A second copy records Fukuda’s demand for a complete 1935 business plan.
subfiles.summary: Fukuda refuses postponement and quota revision; company representatives protest the financial commitment.

subfiles.title: File note on Coe’s enclosures
subfiles.about: A handwritten filing note refers to enclosures with Coe’s letter.
subfiles.summary: The note appears to concern handling Coe’s enclosures.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgement of Coe’s December 14 letter
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges the interview notes and hopes continued efforts will produce acceptable modifications.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Coe and welcomes signs of a more temperate Japanese position.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1073
subfiles.about: The Division summarizes Tokyo’s report on 1935 plans, quotas, and Japanese unease over oil storage rules.
subfiles.summary: Japan initially demanded complete plans but accepted conditional submissions. Japanese companies also struggled with stockholding costs.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch No. 1073 on American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports negotiations over foreign companies’ 1935 plans and signs of weakening support for Japan’s stockholding rules.
subfiles.summary: Fukuda demanded immediate complete plans and threatened penalties, but Yoshino and Kurusu offered a conditional filing arrangement. After consultation with diplomats and head offices, the foreign companies submitted provisional plans with reservations. Grew reports that Japanese firms also faced high storage costs and sought higher gasoline prices; he encloses interview notes and Neville’s conversation memorandum.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: notes of Yoshino–Kurusu interview
subfiles.about: The enclosure records Japanese proposals on trade guarantees, refining, quotas, and conditional plans.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino says foreign companies may retain existing trade and pursue refining without discrimination, although current quotas stand. Kurusu asks for concrete evidence that stockholding costs would force withdrawal or reduced trade. Yoshino agrees to accept 1935 returns conditioned on the companies’ ability to continue operating.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Neville conversation with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Kurusu tells Neville that Japanese oil companies also dislike the storage requirements.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu describes Hashimoto’s reversal on the law and suggests united action by oil companies.

subfiles.title: Atherton telegram No. 628 on British views
subfiles.about: Atherton reports the Foreign Office’s preferred sequence for diplomatic representations and company talks.
subfiles.summary: British officials want senior embassy representatives to tell Japan that its November 20 suggestions are insufficient, then leave written memoranda. They would consider bringing company leaders from Shanghai into talks if Japan shows flexibility. The Foreign Office worries about company threats that British, American, and Dutch firms could not jointly carry out.

subfiles.title: Department telegram to London on proposed Tokyo procedure
subfiles.about: The Department asks London to relay its conditional approval of coordinated informal representations.
subfiles.summary: Grew may proceed with Clive and the oil interests’ support; the ambassadors will decide whether to mention company envoys.

subfiles.title: Department telegram No. 210 to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department authorizes coordinated informal representations and discusses possible direct talks with oil company representatives.
subfiles.summary: Grew is to clarify British plans with Clive. If both embassies and American oil interests agree, he may deliver the proposed oral points. The Department still favors direct company talks because the firms can document the economic burden of stockholding; Grew and Clive may decide whether to raise the envoys’ presence in Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram No. 283 on consultation with Clive
subfiles.about: Grew reports Clive’s agreement on procedure and plans to consult local oil representatives.
subfiles.summary: Clive supports informal representations; both embassies will seek the companies’ views.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Grew telegram No. 283
subfiles.about: A second copy reports agreement with Clive on informal representations.
subfiles.summary: The embassies plan to consult local company representatives before approaching Japan.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram No. 284 on message to Goold
subfiles.about: Grew relays a request for Goold’s agreement to the planned embassy representations and possible company talks.
subfiles.summary: The embassies expect to approach Japanese officials on December 27 or 28 and may suggest discussions with company directors in Shanghai. Grew says Standard-Vacuum representatives have been kept informed.

subfiles.title: Coe letter on the Shanghai representatives’ concerns
subfiles.about: Coe forwards a Shanghai cable and reports that Standard-Vacuum representatives are waiting for instructions.
subfiles.summary: Coe says Walden and Parker agree with Godber on needed changes and expect to travel to Japan soon.

subfiles.title: Incoming cablegram from Walden and Parker
subfiles.about: Walden and Parker ask whether Washington’s view has changed and urge that future company negotiations remain possible.
subfiles.summary: The envoys await Washington’s action and seek clarity about the governments’ intentions.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply to Coe on government policy
subfiles.about: Hornbeck clarifies that U.S. policy is unchanged and that the Department supports further representations and possible direct company talks.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck reviews the embassies’ planned approach and the invitation sent to Goold for comment. He rejects the cable’s implication that the Department opposes direct discussions or has withheld further diplomatic support.

subfiles.title: Department telegram on unchanged oil policy
subfiles.about: The Department asks Tokyo to reassure Standard-Vacuum envoys that naval talks have not changed U.S. oil policy.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo is asked to brief the company’s local representative for confidential relay to Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Atherton despatch No. 1111 forwarding Foreign Office memoranda
subfiles.about: Atherton forwards memoranda of November 27 and December 7 Foreign Office conversations.
subfiles.summary: The cover despatch identifies two enclosed records of Anglo-American oil discussions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of November 27 Foreign Office conversation
subfiles.about: Dooman, Millard, Orde, and Randall discuss coordinated company action against Japanese and Manchurian oil controls.
subfiles.summary: Orde favors effective joint action by British and American oil firms, applying to both Japan and Manchuria, without requiring formal British government action. The discussion explores whether companies could credibly threaten an oil embargo and whether other U.S. suppliers could undercut it. Dooman cautions that such a threat could conflict with U.S. policy against trade barriers.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of December 7 Foreign Office conversation
subfiles.about: U.S. and British officials compare procedures for informal diplomacy and later company negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The British prefer local representatives, backed by Clive, to test Japan’s willingness to concede before senior company envoys leave Shanghai. Dooman describes the American interest in helping those envoys negotiate. Orde favors maintaining intergovernmental contact through the embassies in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram No. 285 on December 27 representations
subfiles.about: Grew reports that both embassies made informal representations and Kurusu welcomed possible company talks.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu responded sympathetically and sought Yoshino’s view before committing to talks with senior oil representatives.
